title: Resolve finalized block queries from the committed XDPoS head
observation: `parse_tag` maps latest, pending, safe and finalized to the same head. The production ChainApi already exposes the QC-committed height through finalized(), but selector parsing does not use it. A request for finalized can therefore select a later, uncommitted block.
fix: Preserve block tags until the chain-aware resolver can distinguish latest from committed finality. Use one coherent chain view for resolution and reads.
Resolve finalized using the committed XDPoS V2 block. Define the V1 and no-commit errors from pinned geth-XDC vectors. Never substitute head when finality is unavailable.
Pin safe behavior to the XDC oracle. XDPoSChain does not expose Ethereum safe-head semantics; reject unsupported tags rather than inventing consensus rules.
Use the resolver for block, state, log-range and fee-history queries. Preserve existing XDC pending behavior; pending is intentionally mapped to latest in the public reference.
accept: With head 105 and committed block 102, finalized resolves to 102 across affected methods.
V1, absent commit, restart and a reorg above the committed floor have explicit vectors.
The fix changes RPC selection only; it does not change fork choice or the committed floor.
related: #42 owns general RPC parity; #33 owns fork choice. Neither records this selector defect.
why: Consumers use finality tags to decide whether a result can still change. Returning the current head overstates finality.

title: Honor requireCanonical and validate EIP-1898 block selectors
observation: `BlockRef::Hash` contains no requireCanonical flag. The object parser accepts blockHash with blockNumber and selects the hash. `state_at` resolves the stored hash without checking whether it is canonical.
fix: Represent the optional canonicality requirement in the typed selector and reject mutually exclusive or mistyped fields.
Check the requested hash against the canonical hash at its height when requireCanonical is true. Hold the same read view through the query.
Keep allowed side-branch queries and typed unsupported-history errors when canonicality is not required. Match the pinned oracle error contract.
accept: A retained side-branch hash with requireCanonical=true is rejected.
Both selector fields, invalid boolean values and invalid hash/quantity encodings are rejected.
A concurrent reorg cannot change the canonicality decision between validation and the state read.
related: #100 pins state during reads; this adds selector validation and canonicality, not another state-pinning implementation.
why: Wallets and indexers use requireCanonical to avoid combining canonical metadata with state from an orphaned block.

Keep the empty default disabled. Specify wildcard, null-origin and credential behavior explicitly. Apply Host checks, namespace policy and authentication independently.

Denied origins receive no permission headers. Vary: Origin prevents cross-origin cache reuse.
Preflight does not execute an RPC method or expose a disabled namespace.
related: #60 owns transport authorization and #171 owns RPC limits. This issue fixes the existing CORS flag that is not wired to HTTP.
why: A browser application cannot use the configured RPC endpoint even when its origin is explicitly allowed.

title: Complete eth_feeHistory percentile and next-block fee semantics
observation: `fee_history` silently drops fractional percentiles, does not validate their order or range, converts zero count to one, narrows gas values through u32, and repeats the last base fee instead of evaluating the next block fee rule. Missing receipts become an empty vector.
fix: Parse and validate numeric percentiles without silently discarding values. Pin ordering, count and error behavior to geth-XDC.
Evaluate the child-height XDC fee rule for the final baseFeePerGas entry. Do not import Ethereum market fees into an XDC chain.
Compute ratios from the full gas values and return a typed history/storage error when required receipts are unavailable.
Replace the documented integer-only and repeated-fee shortcuts with the implemented contract.
accept: Vectors cover fractional, descending, repeated, negative and above-100 percentiles, plus zero count.
A range ending immediately before an XDC fee-rule change returns the correct next fee.
Large gas fields retain correct ratios; missing receipts cannot produce invented reward percentiles.
related: #42 is the parent RPC scope; this issue replaces explicit shortcuts in the current feeHistory implementation.
why: Fee estimators need valid percentile rewards and the next block fee. Silent input changes can produce plausible but incorrect pricing.

Wildcard, OR-topic, empty-filter and bloom false-positive cases remain correct.

title: Add bounded read-only state prefetch before block execution
observation: StateRead mentions read-only prewarming as an intended use, but the repository has no prefetch worker. Disk-backed account and storage reads are demand driven, while run_block executes transactions in order.
fix: Measure cold and warm disk-backed execution before adding workers.
Use a parent-state-pinned read-only view to warm bounded account, storage and code caches from candidate transactions.
Bound workers, queued transactions, reads and cache bytes. Cancel stale work on reorg, parent change, shutdown or execution completion.
Keep canonical writes and publication on the existing execution/import path. Make prefetch optional and treat a miss as a normal read.
accept: Enabled and disabled execution produce identical state, receipts, logs and gas across fork and special-transaction fixtures.
Cancellation releases every state pin and worker; memory remains within its configured budget.
Report disk-backed latency, IO and RSS before/after, including a workload with no benefit.
related: #248 caches analyzed bytecode; #246 hashes tries in parallel; #247 overlaps commit. This issue warms state reads and does not duplicate those changes.
why: Disk latency can stall otherwise sequential execution. Competitor prefetchers move optional reads ahead of the critical path without changing consensus.
loop: Warm only while the parent view remains valid. Discard stale work; never retry without a fresh parent and a budget.

title: Prototype deterministic parallel transaction execution with serial fallback
observation: `run_block` executes its transaction loop sequentially. The accepted scale review calls for a later parallel-EVM prototype behind serial-equivalence and bounded-memory gates. No such executor is currently present.
fix: Keep serial execution as the default and correctness oracle. Introduce an opt-in executor interface with per-transaction speculative overlays.
Track read/write conflicts and validate in block order. Re-execute invalidated work and fall back to serial after a bounded retry budget.
Preserve XDC special transactions, TRC21 routing, wide balances, native hooks, fork transitions and Amsterdam commitments. Serialize operations that cannot be proven independent.
Workers must not publish roots or canonical heads. Measure representative independent and highly contended blocks before proposing a default change.
accept: Serial and parallel paths produce identical receipts, logs, gas, state roots and BAL commitments.
Conflict, revert, deployment, nonce-chain, special-transaction and fork-boundary fixtures pass.
Cancellation, repeated conflicts and worker failure yield bounded cleanup or safe serial fallback.
A replay report includes resource usage and regressions; no throughput claim is accepted without measurements.
related: #7, #10 and #58 provide execution correctness gates. #246 concerns trie hashing, not EVM transaction scheduling.
why: Parallel execution is a competitive performance option for independent transactions. It is a research-to-implementation task, not a claim that XDC semantics can be changed.
loop: Speculate, validate in block order and retry conflicts within a fixed budget. Use serial fallback when the budget is exhausted.

title: Revalidate discovery endpoints and replace dead routing-table entries
observation: Table has no last-bond timestamp or eviction/revalidation state. A full bucket permanently refuses new entries. FindNode accepts a previously stored identity/IP without checking whether its endpoint proof is still recent.
fix: Track bounded endpoint-proof freshness and periodically revalidate routing entries.
Use a bounded replacement cache when a bucket is full; replace dead entries after verified failure.
Require a recent endpoint proof before amplified discovery replies and refresh changed endpoints safely. Preserve the XDC ping encoding.
accept: A full bucket with dead nodes eventually admits verified replacements.
A stale bond cannot authorize a FindNode response until renewed.
A simulated clock and packet-loss test prove bounded retries, memory and refresh traffic.
related: #221 persists peers across restarts. This unit manages freshness and replacement while a node is running.
why: A long-running node can exhaust its routing table with dead endpoints and continue trusting stale endpoint proofs.
loop: Periodically probe a bounded subset. Back off failures, expire proofs and promote verified replacements.

title: Limit subnet concentration in the discovery routing table
observation: Routing-table insertion checks node identity, bucket distance and count, but has no per-subnet diversity accounting. Many identities on one subnet can occupy the bounded table.
fix: Add bounded per-bucket and whole-table subnet accounting for public discovery entries.
Define IPv4 and IPv6 grouping and explicit private-network exceptions without silently granting trust.
Update counters atomically on insertion, replacement and removal, including endpoint changes.
accept: Many distinct identities from one subnet cannot exceed its configured allocation.
Diverse legitimate endpoints remain discoverable.
Replace/remove/change-address tests preserve counts and never bypass total table bounds.
related: #175 restricts allowed CIDRs and #199 restricts peer identities. Diversity limits address concentration among otherwise allowed discovery entries.
why: Identity-count limits alone do not give routing diversity when many public keys share the same network origin.

Advertised IPv6 enodes round-trip through the parser.
IPv4 behavior and separate TCP/UDP ports remain covered.

title: Deduplicate peer redial jobs and bound retry scheduling
observation: Every NetHandle::add_peer call spawns another endless five-second redial loop and appends its handle to a vector. Jobs are not keyed by peer identity, so repeated additions create duplicate long-lived work.
fix: Own one dial intent per peer identity and update it idempotently when addresses or trust settings change.
Bound concurrent dials and retained intents; use bounded backoff with jitter after failures.
Cancel the corresponding job on removal and all jobs on shutdown. Preserve the repository decision that static peers receive trust treatment.
accept: Adding one peer repeatedly leaves one managed intent and one active dial.
A failed endpoint backs off without synchronized retry bursts.
Removal and shutdown release jobs and prevent later redials.
related: #163 and #42 own admin peer methods. This fixes scheduler ownership underneath those methods rather than creating another removePeer API.
why: Duplicate management requests should not consume an increasing number of background tasks or repeated DNS/dial work.
loop: Retry a managed intent with bounded backoff. Stop on removal, connection success until disconnect, or node shutdown.

title: Use a heap for block-builder transaction selection
observation: The builder keeps one head per sender in a vector and scans all heads in best() for every transaction selection. The source explicitly leaves a binary heap for large pending sets.

Preserve per-sender nonce order, special-transaction handling, Shift and Pop behavior.
Measure large multi-sender pools and keep small-pool overhead visible.
accept: The old and new selectors produce identical selections on randomized pools.
Insufficient funds, gas exhaustion, fee changes and special transactions preserve ordering rules.
Selection comparisons scale logarithmically per heap update instead of scanning every sender.
related: #43 implements block production. #250 parallelizes sender recovery; neither changes this selection data structure.
why: Large pools currently add avoidable CPU work to the time-limited block-building path.

title: Serve snap ranges from bounded database views without rebuilding whole-state snapshots

fix: Add a retained-root read interface that streams bounded account/storage ranges and proofs from persisted state/trie tables.
Apply peer and global admission before expensive reads or proof construction.
Bound root metadata, cursor lifetime and proof buffers; avoid whole-state and whole-code-map copies.
Preserve XDC wide-account encoding, empty-root refusal and cryptographic proof verification.
accept: Serving a small range does not allocate memory proportional to total chain state.
Concurrent import remains within the existing latency budget while a peer requests ranges.
Client-side proof validation accepts every served range, including pagination and retained-root boundaries.
related: #145 makes local state and snap installation disk-backed. This distinct server-side path still materializes full snapshots.
why: A memory-bounded follower can lose that property when another node asks it to serve snap data.

title: Serve snap bytecode requests without requiring a warmed root cache
observation: GetByteCodes contains no root. SnapServer selects a root from cache.last() for rootless requests and answers empty when the cache is empty, even though bytecode is available by hash in storage.
fix: Route bytecode requests directly to the retained content-addressed code store.
Enforce hash-count, byte and time budgets without building an account snapshot.
Keep missing-code and empty-code behavior compatible with snap/1 and verify content hashes.
accept: A fresh server answers a known code hash before any account-range request.
Evicting root snapshots does not change bytecode availability.
Unknown, empty-code and oversized query cases follow the protocol limits.
related: #37 owns snap/1. This is the rootless bytecode query path, separate from range-proof streaming.
why: A peer can request code in any valid sync order; it should not need an unrelated query to warm server state first.

title: Fix heartbeat scheduling when the interval exceeds the token-bucket burst
observation: Heartbeat::start creates a bucket with burst 3, then calls try_take with cost equal to interval seconds. TokenBucket documents that a cost above its burst never succeeds. A configured interval greater than three seconds therefore prevents sends in this service loop.
fix: Use consistent token units for heartbeat sends, independent of the interval value.
Schedule the next send from a monotonic deadline without catch-up bursts after long stalls.
Test the actual service loop with an injected clock/transport and keep failures bounded by the configured cadence.
accept: Intervals of 1, 15 and 60 seconds all send according to their documented schedule.
A long pause causes no unbounded catch-up burst.
Transport failures do not create a tight retry loop, and shutdown completes promptly.
related: #41 owns runtime heartbeat integration. This is a deterministic scheduling defect inside the existing service, even before integration.
why: Longer monitoring intervals must reduce traffic rather than silently disable all heartbeats.

title: Run queued transaction expiry from the live pool service
observation: The pool library implements evict_expired, but PoolService only waits for head changes and calls reset. No production caller invokes the expiry routine, so queue lifetime does not trigger removal while the service runs.
fix: Add a bounded monotonic expiry tick to the pool service and run it against a pinned current state.

title: Hold RPC permits until blocking workers stop and account for each cost class
observation: The class semaphore permit is owned by the async serve future, while work runs in spawn_blocking. A timeout or dropped request releases the permit even if the worker is still running. A mixed batch acquires only its highest class semaphore, bypassing lower-class concurrency accounting.
fix: Transfer worker resource permits into the blocking closure so cancellation of the waiting future does not release active capacity.
Account for each executing method class in a batch, or reserve a documented equivalent set of permits without deadlock.
Check cancellation between batch members and inside long operations; instrument actual worker counts separately from waiting requests.
accept: A deliberately slow cancelled handler keeps its permit until it exits.
Repeated timeouts cannot increase running workers beyond configured class bounds.
Mixed-cost batches and ordinary requests respect each class limit.
related: #16 defines budgets. This unit repairs two concrete admission-accounting paths that do not enforce those budgets.
why: A deadline limits waiting time; it does not stop a blocking thread. Releasing capacity early permits more work than the configured limit.
